heuristics.rule: Send cold outreach emails at exactly 7:25 AM on weekdays so they appear at the top of the inbox when professionals check email at 7:30 AM
heuristics.condition: When cold emailing professionals for networking or informational interviews...
heuristics.action: Schedule emails to arrive at 7:25 AM on weekday mornings
heuristics.because: The poster reports that a VP of IR at Blue Apron, who had ignored emails for over a month, finally replied after receiving an email timed this way — the logic being it surfaces at the top of the inbox during the morning email-check habit

heuristics.rule: Tailor your resume twice: once by benchmarking against people in the same role at the same company, and once by searching '[job title] resume' online to see how others in that role frame their experience
heuristics.condition: When updating or tailoring a resume for a specific role or industry pivot...
heuristics.action: Find resumes of people in the same role at the same company AND search publicly available resumes for that job title, then align your language and framing to both
heuristics.because: The poster describes iterating through 10+ drafts using this two-step method and having their final resume called 'perfect' by an NYU career coach

heuristics.rule: After applying online, proactively email at least one HR contact AND one functional leader (e.g. Creative Director) at the company to ensure your application is seen
heuristics.condition: When submitting applications through online portals where visibility is uncertain...
heuristics.action: Find LinkedIn profiles of relevant HR and functional leads, locate their email format, and send a short personalized follow-up email
heuristics.because: One commenter reports this follow-up practice led directly to interview invitations — HR would reply saying they wanted to chat — and credits it as more effective than the online application alone

heuristics.rule: Track every application in a structured system (e.g. OneNote, Excel) with columns for company, role, date applied, source, follow-up status, and interview outcomes
heuristics.condition: When running a high-volume job search across many companies simultaneously...
heuristics.action: Maintain a live tracker to avoid duplicate applications, missed follow-ups, and loss of data needed to calculate conversion rates
heuristics.because: Two separate posters independently describe using tracking systems; one notes it was how she calculated her final 1/200 offer ratio, and the other references a professor-provided Excel template as standard practice

heuristics.rule: Apply to summer internships at the start of grad school (fall semester), not in spring — recruiting for next summer begins immediately in the fall
heuristics.condition: When entering a 2-year US graduate program with intent to stay in the US after graduation...
heuristics.action: Begin attending info sessions, career fairs, and applying for internships in the first semester of grad school
heuristics.because: The poster explicitly states she arrived not knowing recruiting timelines and missed the entire summer intern cycle, which often yields return offers — she describes this as a costly mistake

heuristics.rule: Use the STAR format (Situation, Task, Action, Result) for all behavioral interview questions
heuristics.condition: When preparing for behavioral interviews at US companies...
heuristics.action: Structure every story-based answer using the STAR framework to make responses easier for recruiters to follow
heuristics.because: Multiple commenters independently note career coaches universally recommend this structure; the first poster confirms it as the primary feedback from NYU career coaching sessions

heuristics.rule: To find a corporate contact's email when it isn't public, identify the company's email format from a publicly visible contact page, then apply that format to the name found on LinkedIn
heuristics.condition: When trying to reach a specific person at a company for a cold outreach or follow-up...
heuristics.action: Find any public-facing email at the company (e.g. from a contact or press page) to reverse-engineer the format (firstname@company.com, etc.), then construct the target person's email
heuristics.because: One commenter describes this as a core step in their outreach workflow and notes that most companies use consistent email formats

decision_factors.why_it_matters: STEM OPT extension grants 3 years of work authorization; non-STEM OPT is limited to 1 year, dramatically narrowing the employer pool and the time buffer for job searching
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check whether your specific program appears on the official STEM designated degree program list maintained by DHS; do not assume by field name alone

decision_factors.factor: Timing of OPT application relative to graduation
decision_factors.why_it_matters: OPT processing can take 2-3+ months; applying too late means arriving at graduation without work authorization and missing time-sensitive job offers
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Count backward 90 days from graduation date — that is the earliest you can apply; check USCIS processing times regularly as they fluctuate

decision_factors.factor: Quality vs. quantity of networking contacts
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A referral requires the referrer to fill out forms, vouch for you, and invest reputational capital — casual coffee chats do not produce referrals unless there is a genuine connection and demonstrated competence
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask whether the contact has a concrete basis for vouching for your work (they've seen your output, worked with you, or you've had substantive exchanges) — not just whether they were friendly

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Applying to non-sponsoring companies wastes application effort and creates false pipeline signals; the pool of sponsors is smaller than the total job market
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Use myvisajobs.com to verify sponsorship history; use school career portals that pre-filter for sponsors when available

decision_factors.factor: Industry type relative to networking necessity
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Finance roles depend heavily on alumni networks and referrals due to high competition and relationship-driven hiring; other industries have less dependency on networking for entry-level roles
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Research what proportion of entry-level hires in your target industry come through referrals vs. direct applications; talk to people already working in those roles

decision_factors.factor: Whether you have prior US work experience or internships
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Entry-level job descriptions frequently require 3-5 years of experience (the 'catch-22' the poster names), making prior US internships a de facto filter for many roles
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Audit your resume for US-based work experience; if absent, prioritize internship applications and school projects that can be framed as professional experience

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Delaying OPT application because you're unsure if you'll job search in the US
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You may receive a job offer before your OPT card arrives and be forced to decline it — there is no way to accelerate USCIS processing once submitted
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who are undecided about staying in the US until late in their final semester — they lose the optionality they thought they were preserving

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing a non-STEM graduate program because it aligns with your interests
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You get only 1 year of OPT instead of 3, dramatically shortening your runway for H-1B lottery eligibility and increasing pressure on the job search timeline
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students in humanities, communications, design, or social sciences who did not research visa implications before choosing their program

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on a promised referral or reference letter from a professor or contact
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Professionals who verbally commit to helping frequently go silent without warning — professors stop responding, LinkedIn contacts ghost after agreeing to coffee chats
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who build their job search strategy around a few high-value introductions rather than maintaining parallel outreach pipelines

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Focusing on networking events and coffee chats as the primary job search method
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Networking without demonstrable skills or a compelling reason for someone to refer you produces social contact but not referrals — referrers must fill out detailed forms and stake their reputation
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students in fields where their skills are not immediately visible (non-portfolio fields) or who have not yet built a track record the referrer can point to

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a less-than-ideal US job to stay on OPT rather than returning home
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If you ultimately plan to return to your home country, a low-quality US work experience may not transfer well — the domain knowledge, network, and career trajectory may not align with the home market
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who are ambivalent about long-term US residency but stay for the credential, ending up with experience that doesn't compound in either market

failure_patterns.pattern: Applying to jobs online for months without any parallel networking, skill-building, or strategic targeting — treating job search as a volume game with no feedback loops
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Online applications feel productive and low-risk; rejection is delayed and anonymous, so the activity continues without forcing a strategic reassessment
failure_patterns.consequence: The poster reports sending ~200 applications over 132 days post-graduation before receiving a single offer — a ratio she describes as 'heartbreaking'
warning_signs: Applying to 10+ jobs per day with no customization
No follow-up emails sent after applications
No tracking system to identify which approaches produce responses

failure_patterns.pattern: Starting the job search too late in a grad program — not attending info sessions or recruiting events in the first semester
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: New arrivals prioritize settling in and socializing; no one in their network explains that recruiting for next summer begins immediately in the fall semester
failure_patterns.consequence: Missing the entire summer internship recruiting cycle, which is often the highest-yield path to a full-time offer via return offer
warning_signs: Not signed up for career center email lists in the first month
No awareness of what a 'recruiting season' is or when it starts
Assuming job search starts after graduation

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating a coffee chat as sufficient to generate a referral, without giving the contact a concrete reason to advocate for you
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students are told 'networking is everything' without understanding that referrals require reputational investment from the referrer — a 30-minute meeting does not establish that
failure_patterns.consequence: Contacts are friendly but do not follow through on implicit referral expectations; students interpret this as the contact being unhelpful rather than recognizing the relationship was insufficiently developed
warning_signs: Asking for a referral after a single meeting
No follow-up thank-you email after coffee chats
Unable to articulate what specific value you'd bring to the contact's company

failure_patterns.pattern: Failing to develop analytical or technical skills because your undergraduate major didn't require them, then discovering they are the primary filter in hiring
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students assume their communication or subject-matter skills are sufficient and don't recognize until late in grad school that US employers expect quantifiable, tool-based skills (SQL, Excel, Bloomberg, etc.)
failure_patterns.consequence: Being screened out at resume review stage for roles that require technical skills; the poster describes this as a structural disadvantage she couldn't fully overcome
warning_signs: Resume has no skills section or only lists soft skills
JDs consistently require tools you've never used
Being filtered out before any human review

failure_patterns.pattern: Not checking whether a company sponsors visas before investing significant application and networking effort
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The natural job search workflow focuses on role fit and company appeal; visa sponsorship feels like a later-stage concern but actually eliminates many companies upfront
failure_patterns.consequence: Wasted effort on companies that will reject candidates requiring sponsorship at the offer stage, often without transparency earlier in the process
warning_signs: Not using myvisajobs.com or equivalent as part of initial company research
Applying to small startups or companies with no prior H-1B filing history
Discovering sponsorship policy only when an offer is imminent or declined

diagnostic_questions.question: Is your degree program on the STEM designated degree program list?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether you have 12 or 36 months of OPT work authorization — a 3x difference in runway for job searching and H-1B lottery attempts
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Are you on track to apply for OPT at least 90 days before graduation to ensure the card arrives in time?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Have you scoped your job search to companies with a strong sponsorship track record, given that you'll need to secure a role quickly within a 1-year window?

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you identified specific companies that have previously sponsored H-1B visas for your role type?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals whether the candidate is targeting strategically or applying broadly, including to companies that will not sponsor — which is a major time sink
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you cross-referenced this list with job openings and begun building any contacts at those companies?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Start with myvisajobs.com and your school's career portal sponsorship filter before expanding your target list

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your current application-to-interview conversion rate?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: If below roughly 5-10%, it signals a resume or targeting problem, not a market problem — and requires diagnosis before continuing to apply at volume
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If you're getting interviews but no offers, the problem is interview preparation or positioning — not volume
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If you have no data because you haven't been tracking, that is itself the first problem to fix

diagnostic_questions.question: Are the skills listed on your resume the same skills explicitly named in the job descriptions you're applying to?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: ATS systems filter on keyword match; a mismatch means your resume may not be seen by a human regardless of your actual qualifications
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Are the skills also demonstrated through specific quantified accomplishments, or just listed?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Use a job description keyword matching tool (e.g. Jobscan) and revise resume before next application batch

diagnostic_questions.question: When did you start attending recruiting events and applying for internships relative to your program start date?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals whether the candidate missed early-cycle opportunities (summer internships, return-offer pathways) that are disproportionately high-yield for international students
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If you have an internship, did you receive or pursue a return offer?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If you're now in your final year with no internship experience, pivot to targeting companies with rolling hiring or that explicitly hire new grads without prior US internships

industry_realities.common_belief: Networking (coffee chats, LinkedIn outreach, events) is the most important job search activity and will lead to referrals
industry_realities.actual_reality: Networking is necessary but not sufficient — referrals require the referrer to fill out detailed forms and stake their professional reputation; a single coffee chat rarely produces one. The poster explicitly caps networking's importance at 60% and emphasizes that meaningful relationships, not volume of contacts, drive referrals
industry_realities.implication: Students should invest in building demonstrated competence and a clear value proposition before pursuing networking, not use networking as a substitute for it

industry_realities.common_belief: Entry-level jobs are accessible without prior professional experience if you have the right degree
industry_realities.actual_reality: Many entry-level job descriptions in the US require 3-5 years of experience — the poster explicitly calls this a 'catch-22' — making prior internships (especially US-based ones) a de facto requirement for competitiveness
industry_realities.implication: Students should prioritize any internship opportunity, even unpaid or tangentially relevant, to break the experience catch-22 early rather than waiting for an ideal role

industry_realities.common_belief: You can search for jobs effectively using just LinkedIn and one or two job boards
industry_realities.actual_reality: Different job boards surface different openings; direct company website applications, school career portals (which filter for sponsors), and cold outreach to non-posting companies each access different portions of the opportunity pool
industry_realities.implication: A comprehensive search requires combining multiple channels — school portal, LinkedIn, Indeed, Glassdoor, direct company sites, and cold email to companies not actively posting

industry_realities.common_belief: English proficiency is the main barrier to getting hired as an international student
industry_realities.actual_reality: One commenter with direct US hiring experience explicitly states 'English level really doesn't matter, but being able to communicate does' — interviewers expect non-native fluency and focus instead on core skills and differentiated experience
industry_realities.implication: International students should stop self-selecting out of opportunities due to language insecurity and instead focus energy on skill demonstration and preparation

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Attends networking events and coffee chats to 'meet people' and hopes referrals will follow naturally from being likable
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Treats each networking interaction as 'professional stalking' — researches the person deeply before reaching out, prepares specific questions, delivers a clear value exchange, and follows up with a targeted thank-you email referencing specific conversation points
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Without a strategic approach, networking produces social contacts but not referrals; the referral mechanism requires the other person to have a concrete basis for vouching for you

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Writes one resume, gets it reviewed once, and submits it widely
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Iterates through 10+ versions, seeks feedback from people actually working in the target role and industry, benchmarks against real resumes of people in the same position, and maintains multiple versions for different role types
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A resume that doesn't 'speak the language' of the target industry's recruiters gets filtered out before human review; industry insiders recognize the framing patterns

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they manage the OPT timeline
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Waits until after graduation or until certain about staying before applying for OPT, treating it as a post-decision administrative step
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Applies for OPT 90 days before graduation regardless of certainty about plans, because processing time is fixed and irreversible — missing an offer due to no OPT card is a known failure mode
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: One poster in this thread directly lost a summer internship offer because her OPT card hadn't arrived yet — a preventable outcome

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Treats each rejection as evidence of personal inadequacy; gets stuck in emotional processing and reduces application activity
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Treats job search as a numbers game with a known conversion ratio (~1 offer per 100-200 applications in competitive markets); uses rejection data to identify patterns rather than as personal feedback
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Emotional responses to rejection reduce the volume and quality of effort at exactly the point when consistency is most important

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Waits until hired to learn tools and skills required by the role
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Reads JDs actively to identify skill gaps and fills them during the search period; adds skills to resume as they are acquired, treating the search period as productive learning time
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The job search period can last 3-5+ months; candidates who skill up during this time arrive at interviews more competitive than those who wait

community_misconceptions.misconception: You can travel internationally while waiting for your OPT card as long as you plan to come back before it expires
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Students assume that because they are still in valid F-1 status, travel is permitted during OPT application processing — the restriction feels like an administrative technicality rather than a hard rule
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: USCIS guidance and DSO advice is to avoid international travel while your OPT application is pending; re-entry requires both an approved OPT EAD card AND a job offer documentation — without both, re-entry can be denied
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: A student who travels during pending OPT processing may be denied re-entry to the US, effectively ending their job search and forfeiting any pending applications

community_misconceptions.misconception: Getting a coffee chat with someone means they'll refer you if you ask
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Networking advice is often framed as 'build relationships and referrals will follow' — students interpret any positive interaction as an implicit commitment to help
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Referrals require the referrer to complete detailed forms and stake their professional reputation; they only do this for people they have a specific, concrete reason to vouch for — a 30-minute coffee chat does not create that basis
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Students wait for referrals that never come, lose time, and blame the contact rather than recognizing the relationship needed more substantive development

community_misconceptions.misconception: Non-STEM students have roughly the same job market access as STEM students, just with fewer tech roles
community_misconceptions.why_believed: The OPT difference (1 year vs. 3 years) is discussed primarily in immigration contexts, not career strategy contexts — students don't realize it affects employer willingness to hire them at all
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: A 1-year OPT window means only one H-1B lottery attempt before authorization expires; many employers avoid non-STEM international candidates entirely because the sponsorship timeline is too tight. The poster explicitly describes this as severely limiting her options
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Non-STEM students apply to a much larger pool of companies than will realistically consider them, wasting effort and creating false confidence in their pipeline

real_case_outcomes.situation: Non-STEM graduate student in communications/media, no analytical skills, no prior US internship, graduated from a US grad program and began job searching post-graduation
real_case_outcomes.decision: Ran a high-volume cold outreach and application campaign (~200 applications), maintained detailed tracking in OneNote, attended networking events, conducted coffee chats, and iterated resume through 10+ drafts with industry insiders
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Received one offer after 132 days post-graduation and approximately 200 applications — a 0.5% conversion rate. Described the process as involving repeated breakdowns, insomnia, and avoiding calls with family
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Non-STEM international students face compounding disadvantages (1-year OPT, no technical skills, no US internship history) that make job search significantly harder than for STEM peers — volume alone is insufficient; the structural disadvantages must be addressed proactively during the degree program

real_case_outcomes.situation: Undergraduate student who was undecided about US job search and delayed OPT application until late April (graduation in mid-May)
real_case_outcomes.decision: Applied for OPT in late April expecting quick processing; received a job offer in late May before OPT card arrived
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Had to decline the summer internship offer because she lacked work authorization. Did not receive her OPT card until August — approximately 3 months after graduation
real_case_outcomes.lesson: OPT processing takes 2-3+ months; even if you're uncertain about staying, apply at the 90-day-before-graduation window to preserve optionality — you cannot accelerate USCIS processing

real_case_outcomes.situation: Design student searching for a position at a specific company with no publicly posted opening and no known contacts there
real_case_outcomes.decision: Found a company alumni on LinkedIn (the Global Chief Creative Officer), sent a cold connection request and email referencing the shared school connection
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Received an interview invitation from the company's recruiter within two days and ultimately received an offer
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Alumni connections — even to very senior people — can shortcut the formal application process; the shared institutional identity creates enough of a hook to prompt action even from executives

psychological_barriers.trigger: Being deep into a 3-5 month job search with no offers, OPT grace period approaching, and avoiding telling family about the situation
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Shame-driven isolation — the belief that not having a job is a personal failure that reflects on family investment and cultural expectations, making honest communication feel too costly
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Avoiding calls home, not asking for help, pretending everything is fine while privately breaking down; the poster describes insomnia, full-day paralysis, and crying alone rather than seeking support
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Normalize the timeline — 3-6 months post-graduation is statistically common for international students, not a signal of failure. Reframe family calls as emotional support rather than status reports to reduce the shame loop

psychological_barriers.trigger: Having a coffee chat go well and then waiting passively for the contact to follow up with referral or opportunities
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Avoidance of rejection — following up feels presumptuous or needy, so students wait passively rather than risk being told no explicitly
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Students do not send follow-up emails, do not ask directly for referrals, and interpret silence as the contact being 'busy' rather than recognizing they need to maintain the relationship actively
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe follow-up as professional courtesy, not as asking for a favor — a thank-you email the next day is expected etiquette, not an imposition. Normalize that contacts are busy and that a prompt, specific follow-up is what keeps you visible

psychological_barriers.trigger: Receiving consecutive rejections or no responses after a large application batch
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Sunk cost and learned helplessness — the energy already invested in applications makes stopping or changing strategy feel like wasting prior effort; repeated rejection creates a generalized sense that the system is fixed against you
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Continuing to apply in the same way at the same volume rather than diagnosing the conversion problem; refusing to seek resume or interview feedback because it might confirm the fear of being unqualified
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe job search as a measurement problem, not a judgment problem — low conversion rate is diagnostic data, not a verdict. Introduce a structured review of where in the funnel candidates are dropping (no response = resume problem; no offer after interviews = interview problem)

psychological_barriers.trigger: Feeling too introverted or anxious to attend networking events, choosing to apply online instead
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Social anxiety combined with a cognitive distortion that online applications are an equivalent substitute for in-person relationship-building
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Students rationalize staying home as 'applying more efficiently' when the actual driver is avoidance of social discomfort; the poster names this pattern directly ('I want to stay home, watch Netflix, why do I have to meet people I don't know')
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Acknowledge the discomfort is real while clarifying that the discomfort is the cost of entry, not a signal to avoid the activity — and that each event gets easier with practice. Suggest low-stakes starting points (small alumni dinners, virtual events) before large career fairs

reframing_moves.original_framing: I need to network more — I should go to more events and have more coffee chats to find a job
reframing_moves.reframe: Networking is not about volume of contacts — it's about whether you can give someone a specific, concrete reason to stake their reputation on you. Ask yourself: why would a person who met you 30 minutes ago fill out a referral form for you?
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts focus from activity (attending events) to outcome (building a credible case for referral), which forces candidates to honestly assess whether they have a compelling enough value proposition before expecting referrals
reframing_moves.example_language: Refer别人很烦的，要填一堆表格… 你真的有那么好值得refer嘛

reframing_moves.original_framing: I can't find a job — the market is bad / companies don't want to sponsor / I'm not good enough
reframing_moves.reframe: Job search is a numbers game with a known conversion ratio. If you've sent 200 applications and have 1 offer, that's 0.5% — which is actually a data point, not a verdict on your worth. The question is: where is the funnel breaking down?
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Converts a shame narrative ('I'm not good enough') into a diagnostic problem ('where in the process am I losing people'), which is actionable and emotionally less paralyzing
reframing_moves.example_language: 找工作是个numbers game，意思是你投大概15封简历能有一个面试，投100封简历，说不定能有一个offer

reframing_moves.original_framing: No one is helping me — my professor stopped replying, my contacts are ghosting me
reframing_moves.reframe: No one has an obligation to help you. People are busy and you are not their priority. The only reliable variable in your job search is your own effort. Build a system that doesn't depend on any single person following through.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Removes the victim frame and the dependency on others, replacing it with a self-reliance frame that is both psychologically empowering and practically correct — parallel pipelines are more robust than single-thread relationships
reframing_moves.example_language: 没有人有义务帮你，所以虽然相信人性是好的，但是要知道大家都很忙，no one gives a fuck。靠自己，最靠谱

reframing_moves.original_framing: I should wait until I'm sure I want to stay in the US before applying for OPT
reframing_moves.reframe: Applying for OPT is not a commitment to stay — it's buying optionality. You can always choose not to use it. But if you don't apply early, you cannot retroactively recover the months of processing time you lost.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Reframes OPT application as a low-cost insurance decision rather than a high-stakes life commitment, which removes the psychological barrier of premature certainty
reframing_moves.example_language: 最好是毕业前90天开始申请… 我拖到四月底才决定申请OPT… 因此，我在五月底有幸拿到一份实习offer时，因为没有OPT而完美错过了这份Summer Intern
